fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says he acted according to what is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses. There the LORD commanded, “…each is to die for his own sin.” So the murderers' sons live.

That's it, baker. The text says he hired 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel for a hundred talents of silver. Three hundred thousand soldiers of his own, and he still goes shopping for more. I know that feeling, like having a whole tray of cookies and still reaching for another batch of dough.

Moab? Nope, that one's not in this verse. The text says the 100,000 mighty men of valor came from Israel, hired for a hundred talents of silver. I'd say pack your bags and head back to the verse, friend. Those hired troops are right there waiting for you.
Egypt? Friend, that's a long way to go for a hire. The text says he hired 100,000 mighty men of valor from Israel. The price was a hundred talents of silver, so somebody got a nice paycheck.

That's the reason, baker. The man of God says, “…the LORD is not with Israel—not with any of the Ephraimites.” The reason he gives isn't about the soldiers' skill. It's about the LORD not being with Israel.

I see why you'd think so, since bravery sounds like it should count. But the man of God says the opposite. He says, “Even if you go and fight bravely in battle, God will overthrow you before the enemy…” So the answer is False. Courage can't change what he says about going with Israel's troops, because “…God has power to help and power to overthrow.”
Patient? Oh, friend, no. The text says they were furious with Judah and returned home in great anger. Hired for a job, then sent home. I think a calm sigh and a shrug is not what happened here.

That's what the text says, baker. The troops he had dismissed raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon. They struck down 3,000 people and carried off a great deal of plunder. It's a hard turn in the story.

They went home, but staying quiet isn't what the text shows. It says the troops Amaziah dismissed raided the cities of Judah, from Samaria to Beth-horon. They struck down 3,000 people and carried off a great deal of plunder. This part of the story is heavy.

That's it, baker. The text says the prophet stopped, but he said, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my advice.” He quits talking, but he still gets that last word in. I think that takes some nerve.

No words at all? Not quite, friend. The text says the prophet stopped, but he said, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my advice.” He gets one last sentence in.

Not that word, friend. The prophet says, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not heeded my advice.” It's a hard word, and the text gives two reasons for it. Amaziah did this, and he did not heed the prophet's advice.
